A friend's bad experience made me want to write and research more on this. I hope this research helps him and has him succeed in his next interview.
First, a lot of research needs to be done before the interview. Do your homework and find out as much as you can about the company and the job. Go further than just a quick look at the website. This will be useful when you are being asked questions. The job specifications should be studied carefully.

Second, preparation and rehearsal are to be prioritized. Make sure preparation for likely questions is involved. Rehearse interview questions by yourself. Then, get a friend to ask you questions. Have them give you feedback on your answers. These are the best ways to manage your nerves.
Thirdly, questions about certain skills or experience are going to be asked. Have two to three successful stories up your sleeve. Make them work for you by making sure they focus on results.

On the day of the interview, make sure you're punctual. Punctuality is seen as a sign of professionalism. Also, stay focused. It goes without saying that a successful interview is closely linked with being focused and displaying just the right amount of self-confidence.
Finally, make them believe you. Be yourself and do not pretend. And, before the interview is finished, ask a few smart final questions. The questions should be focused on the company and what the interviewers consider to be crucial skills for the job.

Now, ace your interview and get hired!

In English, all sentences are in either “active” or “passive” voice.

The active voice focuses on the thing which is doing the action (i.e. the subject of the sentence) and the thing receiving the action (i.e. the object). Most sentences in English are in the active voice.
• We need to do a lot of research before the interview.
We use the passive when the ‘doer' (agent) of the action it not so important. We are not interested in knowing who did the action. Our attention is on the object.
• A lot of research needs to be done before the interview.
Here's some more information about the passive of modal verbs.

1. The Passive is formed by [thing receiving the action] + be + past participle + (by) + (thing doing the action)
  2. The passive can be used when the “doer” is unknown, irrelevant, or you want to be vague about who is responsible for the action.
  3. You can also use the passive to talk about a general truth.

You use a causative verb when you want to talk about something that someone else did for you or for another person. It means that the subject caused the action to happen, but didn't do it themselves.
You use the causative verbs get, make and have when you want to make it clear that the subject paid, asked, or persuaded the other person to do something.
• His bad experience made me want to write and research more on this.
The structure of the causative is:

have + person + verb
make + person + verb
get + person + to + verb
Sometimes, you use get when you want to convey the feeling that you need to convince someone to do something. Have is a little more neutral.
